# dsh-chat-eraser

Delete a whole chat session from the sidebar's `...` menu, and delete a single
turn from the transcr

ipt's turn tail. A DeepSeek Harness (dsh) plugin: the host
half performs the durable removal, the br
owser half owns both affordances.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
## Why a plugin is needed

The harness has no deletion API at any layer. `dsh-session-persistence-jsonl`
states it plainly — *"

Nothing deletes session files"* — and the Workspace
browser documents *"sessions can be archived but

never deleted"*. There is no
"delete turn" operation anywhere either: a session is an append-only J

leted"*. There is no
"delete turn" operation anywhere either: a session is an append-only JSONL log.

This plugin is therefore the outside-the-seam operator tool: it edits the same
per-session artifacts
an operator would, and it does so carefully.
## Features

**Delete a session.** The sidebar row's `...` menu gains a *Delete session* row
(placed after the sh

ipped *Archive session*, behind a separator). Confirming, in
this order:

* asks the host to **stop whatever is running in the session** (the registry's
own stop fan-out, the

same one Archive-with-stop uses),
* **takes the session out of the harness's live session store** —

this is the
step that actually removes it. A mounted session is listed from that store, so
a sessio

n deleted out from under it kept its sidebar row *and* kept its log
open, which is why the next prom

pt failed with
`ENOENT … session.v4.jsonl.zstd`. The store's own single-shot removal is
idempotent,

drops the store entry and its attachment, and announces
`session/disposed`, which is what makes the

list and the query drop their live
rows,
* asks the host to **archive it** through its registry API,

so even a stale
client list cannot render the row,
* removes every canonical generation in the sess

ion's directory
(`session[.vN].jsonl[.zstd]`),
* removes its projection-cache checkpoint
(`$DSH_HOME

/storages/session_projcache/sessions/<id>.json`),
* and, when the host refused to archive it, falls

back to scrubbing the
host-durable Workspace registry
(`$DSH_HOME/storages/workspace.json`: workspac

e membership plus the archived
and pinned sets), with a timestamped copy of that file taken first.

A copy of the session log is written into this plugin's own backup tree before
anything is removed.

The removal is complete: the session is gone from the
list data itself, not hidden by the archived f

ilter, and the harness can no
longer mount it — so there is no row to open and no prompt that can fa

il
against a missing file.

Nothing reloads the page. The store release and the archived-state change both
reach the open page t

hrough the host's own events, so the row leaves in place;
an earlier build reloaded here, which flas

hed the empty New Session view and
then brought the row straight back from the harness's in-memory l

the empty New Session view and
then brought the row straight back from the harness's in-memory list.

**Delete a turn.** Every turn in the transcript carries a *Delete turn*
control. Confirming removes

that turn **and every later turn** from the session

## Verified behaviour
| Check | Result |
| Menu row and per-turn control render in the real app | verified in Chromium against a live harness

|
| Session deletion removes the row from the list data, mounted or not | verified: `mounted false`

, `queryListed false`, row gone, still gone after a reload |
| The harness can no longer mount a del

eted session | verified (`mounted false` after deleting the session it had opened) |
| Turn cut on a

621-row, 17-turn session | kept 612 rows, dropped 9, 235,023 → 119,721 bytes |
| Backups before eve

ry rewrite | written to `$DSH_HOME/chat-eraser/backups/` |
| Harness re-reads the rewritten log | af

ter a host restart the transcript renders turns 5..16 (turn 17 gone) |
| Running turn | refused with
code `turn-running` |

`node test/run.mjs` runs the package's checks: the physical codec against a real
session artifact, b

oth deletion operations against a fixture harness home, the
HTTP surface through a stub web server,

and the browser bundle through a stub
module loader.
## What the running harness does and does not see

The harness builds its session list in memory from the persisted corpus **plus
every session it has

mounted**, and it never re-reads a log it already loaded.
That splits the two features:

* **A deleted session** leaves the list immediately: the deletion path archives
it through the host'

s own registry API first, and nothing reloads the page.
* **A cut turn** cannot always be shown imme

diately: the transcript you are
reading is served from the session the harness mounted, so it keeps

showing
the removed turn until the harness is reopened. The rewrite itself is already
durable, and t

he plugin says so rather than pretending — the check runs in the
page right after the operation and

in says so rather than pretending — the check runs in the
page right after the operation and reports

> **Already deleted** — The turn was removed from the log, but this harness
> keeps serving the copy

it mounted when it opened the session, so the
> transcript still shows it. Closing and reopening De

epSeek Harness refreshes
> the transcript.

The same notice appears if a *stale* control is used — clicking delete on a
turn the view still offe

rs but the log no longer has answers `unknown-turn`,
which the client reports as the stale view it i
s, not as a failure.
Reopening the harness loses nothing: no deletion has to be repeated.
## Uptake of a plugin's own code changes
Two halves age differently, which matters when this package is edited in place:

* the **browser half** is watched: the module graph republishes a bundle
revision when `client/clien

t.js` changes, so a page refresh picks it up;
* the **host half** is not: this profile runs HMR with

`root: []`, which keeps
module watching off, and Node caches an imported module for the life of the

process. Edited `lib/*` code therefore takes effect on the next harness
start, while configuration

changes (patch layers, the profile manifest) still
recompose live.
